query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high‐entropy alloy nanoscale multilayers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is primarily governed by interfacial barriers that are enhanced by short‐range order and lattice distortion. Systematically reducing the layer thickness and applying controlled annealing to promote short‐range order will shift the dominant creep mechanism from bulk diffusion‐assisted dislocation climb to interface‐mediated dislocation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coatings composed of alternating FCC and BCC high‐entropy alloy layers, exhibiting compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and initially limited short‐range order at the interfaces.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the individual layer thickness and employ controlled annealing treatments to tune (and enhance) the degree of short‐range order and lattice distortion specifically at the FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.conditions: Sustained loading under creep testing at controlled intermediate to elevated temperatures where the multilayer architecture is maintained without triggering catastrophic phase changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial region between FCC and BCC layers, where the extent of short‐range order and lattice distortion mediate dislocation transmission and diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced short‐range order and increased lattice distortion at the interfaces act as effective barriers to dislocation movement and diffusion. This elevates the activation energy for creep and shifts the deformation mode from one dominated by bulk processes (dislocation climb) to an interface‐mediated mechanism, which provides improved resistance against progressive plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayer samples with decreased layer thickness and annealing-induced elevated short‐range order will exhibit higher creep resistance, indicated by increased activation energies and stress exponents, compared to baseline samples without these treatments.
generation.baseline: Multilayers fabricated without layer thickness variation or post-deposition annealing, which retain lower degrees of short‐range order and mainly rely on bulk dislocation climb for deformation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid under stress and temperature regimes that promote creep without causing microstructural collapse or new phase formation, ensuring that the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thresholds of layer thickness and annealing temperature/time required to achieve a significant interfacial barrier effect are uncertain, and other competing deformation mechanisms may also influence the observed creep behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a set of FCC/BCC multilayer samples where individual layer thickness is systematically varied and controlled annealing is applied to modulate interfacial short‐range order. Subject all samples to creep tests at intermediate to elevated temperatures while monitoring microstructural evolution using high-resolution TEM and diffraction techniques.
measurements: Activation energy and stress exponent derived from creep data
TEM characterization of interfacial structure (short‐range order and lattice distortion)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with reduced layer thickness and enhanced short‐range order do not show statistically significant increases in activation energy or stress exponent (relative to the baseline) and if TEM fails to reveal corresponding increases in interfacial short‐range order, the hypothesis that interfacial barriers govern progressive plastic deformation will be falsified.

Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion. frame.system: High-entropy-alloy multilayers combining FCC and BCC phases, prepared as nanoscale multilayer coatings. The starting state is that of a composite material whose internal structure is characterized by compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and local short-range order.
frame.goal: To develop a testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains progressive plastic deformation (e.g., creep) under sustained loading, including what controls this behavior and under which conditions a given deformation mechanism dominates.
frame.limitation: Conventional deformation frameworks from simple metallic multilayers do not necessarily apply, and preliminary evidence in these high‐entropy systems is insufficient to pinpoint the dominant creep mechanism in FCC/BCC multilayers.
root_cause_cues: insufficient evidence to establish what controls creep

decision.trend: Early HEA creep studies (PMC7512559) sought to adapt conventional dislocation‐climb–controlled mechanisms (rooted in lattice diffusion theories) to high-entropy alloys, but encountered anomalously high stress exponents and activation energies that hinted at additional controlling factors such as severe lattice distortion and evolving short-range order. Subsequent research on dual-phase HEAs (PMC10213035) revealed that the coexistence of FCC and BCC phases introduces interfacial and boundary effects (e.g., coherent precipitate formation and phase boundary barriers) that can significantly alter dislocation mobility. However, none of these investigations directly addressed how such factors behave in the unique context of nanoscale multilayer coatings where the interlayer interfaces may further mediate diffusion and dislocation transmission.
decision.unsolved: In FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers the dominant creep mechanism remains unclear. Specifically, how compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order modulate interfacial versus bulk deformation under sustained loading is unresolved. It is not yet determined whether progressive plastic deformation is primarily governed by altered lattice diffusion and dislocation climb in the individual layers or by interfacial barriers (possibly enhanced by local ordering) that impede dislocation transfer—and under which conditions one response may dominate over the other.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the individual layer thickness and employ controlled annealing treatments to tune the degree of short-range order and lattice distortion at the FCC/BCC interfaces
decision.why: This approach builds on the trend from earlier studies by directly decoupling bulk diffusion effects and interface‐mediated dislocation barriers. By tuning layer thickness and annealing—which affects both the extent of lattice distortion and interface structure—the experiment can reveal whether interfacial conditions control creep progression relative to bulk mechanisms, thus providing a testable hypothesis for the mechanistic origin of progressive plastic deformation in these complex multilayer coatings.
